Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful
push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe

Memory.value: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
Nothing good can happen to me anymore

vignette: Margaret, a 79‑year‑old Irish tailor who has lived most of her life in a small New England town, recalls the night of the bombing of her village in 1944 as if it were a flash that still burns. The image of a red plume of smoke rising from the brick‑faced bakery, the sharp scent of blood on the air, and the muffled screams of men she had sewn uniforms for, remains etched in her mind. Even now, a single word—“battle”—or the sight of a red‑stained seam on a client’s sleeve brings the scene back in a rush of unwanted thoughts. The very presence of blood triggers a cascade of negative beliefs: she feels that happiness has fled from her life, that she is now a hollow shell, and that no good can ever appear on her horizon. These appraisals, in turn, sharpen her confusion over the sequence of the night’s events; she cannot string together the moments of terror, the frantic rush to the nearest shelter, and the lull of dawn. Rage rises with each recollection, as if the memory itself refuses to stay still, and her mind is haunted by the sense that the terror could have been avoided. The dread of hearing friends speak of war and the memory’s vividness reinforce each other, sending her back into the throes of the night whenever she thinks she has escaped it. The disordered recollection of that evening has seeped into Margaret’s everyday life, pulling her into a loop that drives her avoidance of any situation that might stir even a sliver of happiness. She has stopped attending the local quilting club because its bright chatter reminds her of the hopeful moments she no longer can feel. When a close friend offers a warm invitation to a church service, Margaret pushes the thought away, fearing that the joy of the singing might become a painful reminder that she can never feel safe. The same memories that frighten her also make her feel numb and dead inside; she has come to believe that her emotions are unsafe and that they must be pushed away. Each time she rejects a social invitation, she confirms her belief that life offers nothing good, reinforcing the negative view of her future. The memory of the bombing—its blood, its loss, its violence—continues to flare whenever she encounters a red thread or hears a story about soldiers, making her wary of even trivial topics. Her avoidance has seeped into her work: she no longer attends the weekly tailor’s guild meeting, and she has begun to refuse new orders that require bright, cheerful fabrics. The pattern that has become her daily reality is one in which the memory feeds her negative thoughts, which in turn push her further into avoidance, and the cycle tightens as she feels each possibility of joy turning into a threat. It was a quiet morning last week when Margaret, alone in her shop, finally decided that the weight of her thoughts and the constant battle against the memory were too much to bear. She had stopped seeing the faces of friends and felt increasingly isolated from the community that had once surrounded her. The realization that her life had become a series of avoidance rituals—steering clear of positive feelings, rejecting hopeful moments, and shrinking from social contact—made her fear that she was losing herself entirely. The day she chose to call the local counseling center, Margaret clutched the phone with trembling hands, her voice barely a whisper: “I can’t keep doing this. I’m scared of the rage that comes out when I think of that night, and I’m terrified that I’ve lost any chance at happiness.” She hopes to find a way to quiet the intrusive thoughts and to learn how to feel safe again, even in the presence of the colors and sounds that once brought her joy.
